content: The studies reviewed for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines systematically assessed the relationship between household crowding and various health outcomes. Below is a detailed breakdown of the findings and quality assessments for the studies included in the review: 1. Study Focus and Recruitment: Most studies addressed a clearly focused research question and recruited participants in an acceptable manner. This indicates that the studies were designed with a specific aim and followed appropriate methodologies to select their samples. 2. Measurement of Exposure and Outcomes: The majority of studies accurately measured both exposure (e.g., household crowding) and outcomes (e.g., infectious diseases, mental health) to minimize bias. However, a small number of studies were unclear about their methods for measuring these variables, which could introduce potential inaccuracies. 3. Confounding Factors: While many studies identified and accounted for important confounding factors in their analyses, some failed to do so or provided unclear information. This is a critical limitation, as unaddressed confounders can significantly affect the validity of the results. 4. Follow-Up Completeness and Duration: Information on whether the follow-up of study participants was complete and of sufficient duration was often unclear. This is an important consideration, especially for longitudinal studies, as incomplete or short follow-up periods can lead to biased results. 5. Reliability and Applicability of Results: Most studies were deemed to have reliable results that could be applied to local populations. However, a few studies had unclear reliability or limited generalizability due to methodological weaknesses or insufficient reporting. 6. Sample Size and Statistical Analysis: Approximately half of the studies provided a clear description of how their sample size was determined, while others offered only partial or unclear explanations. Similarly, most studies adequately described their statistical analyses, but a minority lacked sufficient detail. 7. Study Participants: The majority of studies provided an adequate description of their participants, which is essential for understanding the context and applicability of the findings. However, some studies failed to do so, limiting the interpretability of their results. 8. Risk of Bias: Studies were assessed for risk of bias across various domains. The domains most frequently identified as being at high risk of bias included the identification and consideration of confounders, reporting of sample size calculations, and descriptions of participant characteristics. Domains with unclear risk of bias often included the adequacy and duration of follow-up. 9. Specific Outcomes: For non-TB infectious diseases, 54 studies were included. Most were of high quality, with reliable results applicable to local populations. However, nine studies had issues with recruitment, and 12 studies were unclear about exposure and outcome measurement. For gastroenteritis and diarrheal diseases, 11 cohort and case-control studies were reviewed. All had at least one domain at high risk of bias, with confounder identification and follow-up adequacy being the most common issues. For mental health outcomes, 13 studies were reviewed. Most were of acceptable quality, with accurate exposure measurement in all but two studies. Statistical analyses were well-described in all but two studies. 10. Studies with High Risk of Bias: Studies identified as having the highest risk of bias included those by Auguet et al. (2016), Chattopadhyay et al. (2016), Mirabel et al. (2015), Sekhar et al. (2009), Phillips et al. (2014), and MacLennan et al. (2006). These studies had significant methodological limitations, such as unclear or incomplete reporting. 11. Studies with Abstract-Only Data: For some studies, only abstract data were available, limiting the ability to fully assess their quality. This highlights the importance of comprehensive reporting in research. 12. High-Quality Studies: Studies that performed well across most domains included those by Alvarado et al. (2016), Baillie et al. (2005), Brander et al. (2017), Doshi et al. (2015), Gares et al. (2017), Grant et al. (2012), Mitra et al. (2018), Olea et al. (2017), Sinha et al. (2015), Tin et al. (2016), and Vincenti-Gonzalez et al. (2017). These studies demonstrated robust methodologies and reliable results. 13. Summary of Findings: Overall, the systematic review highlighted the importance of addressing household crowding as a determinant of health. While most studies were of good quality, methodological weaknesses in some studies underscore the need for rigorous study design and comprehensive reporting to ensure reliable and applicable findings. This detailed analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the quality and findings of studies on household crowding and its health impacts, offering valuable insights for public health policy and future research.
